title: Find Art by Color: How to Use Hex Codes to Land the Perfect Wall Piece
excerpt: How to find art that actually matches your wall color — using hex codes instead of guesswork. No app, no interior designer. Explained step by step.
content:
Most people make one of two expensive mistakes. Either they buy a piece of wall art first, then paint the wall in a color that doesn't work, and spend the weekend at the hardware store with paint swatches. Or they paint the wall first and then buy art that suddenly looks strange next to the fresh tone. Both cost nerves and money.

Finding art by color — systematically, with hex codes — is the relaxed way. No interior designer, no subscription app. Just a bit of tech and three minutes of color theory. Here's how.

First: Why color before art — and not the other way around

Wall paint is cheap per square meter. A good art print isn't. Repainting a room costs you a Saturday and $80 worth of paint. Taking a piece of art back down because it simply doesn't harmonize costs you more — especially on the inside.

The even more important reason: the art is the focal point, the wall is the backdrop. You don't want the backdrop fighting the foreground or, in the end, outshining it.

The wall serves the art, not the other way around. If you choose the wall first, you've already decided which art is even allowed to fit.

My suggestion: if you're planning both from scratch, pick the piece first and paint afterwards. But if your wall is already up and you don't want to repaint it, read on. That's exactly what the rest is about.

Step 1: Find the hex code of your wall

A hex code is a six-character color value, for example #8FA87A for a sage green. It describes a color unambiguously — no matter the device, no matter the shop. Once you have this code, you can search anywhere online for that exact color.

Here's how to find it — free, no install:

Method A: Photo + browser eyedropper

  1. Take a photo of your wall in daylight, no direct sun. No lamp in the frame.
  2. Upload the photo to a site like imagecolorpicker.com — or just open it in a new browser tab.
  3. In Chrome or Firefox: right-click the photo → "Inspect" (or F12). The developer view opens.
  4. At the top of the Elements panel you'll find a small eyedropper icon. Click it, then click on a pixel of your wall in the photo.
  5. The hex code appears automatically. Write it down.

Method B: ColorZilla (browser extension)

ColorZilla is a free extension for Chrome and Firefox. Install it, activate the eyedropper, click anywhere on your screen — and the hex code lands in your clipboard. Faster than method A if you do this often.

Method C: Straight from the paint manufacturer

Still remember which paint you used — say, "Jotun Sage Green 6394"? Then just google the official hex code for it. Many manufacturers publish it on their website. The result is more accurate than any photo, because photos always shift colors a little.

Step 2: Understand color harmony in three minutes

You don't need to take a course in color theory for this. Three terms are enough:

Complementary

Colors that sit opposite each other on the color wheel. Blue and orange. Red and green. Yellow and violet. High contrast, lots of energy. An orange piece in front of a blue wall pulls every eye in the room immediately — great for a statement wall, but it can quickly get exhausting in small rooms.

Analogous

Colors that sit right next to each other on the color wheel. Blue, blue-green, green. Calm, harmonious, natural. Art in tones similar to the wall feels inviting and seamless. Perfect for bedrooms and other retreat spaces.

Triadic

Three colors equidistant from each other on the color wheel — classically yellow, blue and red. Lively but still balanced. The art picks up one or two of these colors, the wall takes the third.

That's enough. You don't need any more theory to get started.

Step 3: Translate the hex code into search terms

Let's say you now have #8FA87A. Head to colorhexa.com and enter the code. On a single page you get:

  • the color name (here: "Moss Green"),
  • matching complementary colors (for deliberate contrast),
  • analogous colors (for soft harmony),
  • a list of similar named colors.

Armed with those names you start searching. "Moss green wall art" turns up harmonious hits. "Rust red wall art" — the complementary color — turns up deliberately contrasting ones.

Step 4: Use an art platform with a real color filter

Most online art shops have no serious color filter. "Blue" as a category is far too crude. You're looking for #8FA87A but can only filter on "green" — and you get neon green, bottle green and everything in between thrown together at random.

Only a few platforms work with precise color search. i-laugh-you is one of them. The whole project consists of a single oil painting that has been cut into 24,236 fragments. Each fragment has its own dominant color palette, directly searchable. Enter your hex code and the system shows you the fragments that match that color exactly.

That's precisely what the design was built for: anyone with a sage green wall shouldn't have to scroll through thousands of irrelevant images. Three clicks — and you're looking at the ten fragments that either pick up your wall color or deliberately push against it.

When to ignore color matching entirely

Basically never. Almost never.

There's exactly one exception: when the art is meant to be the visual shock. A pitch-black piece on a stark white wall. A blazing red statement in an otherwise fully monochrome room. If the piece is supposed to be the conversation anchor for every visitor, it's allowed to break with the wall.

But then that's a deliberate decision, not a happy accident. Anyone who simply hopes randomly chosen contrast will somehow "work" gets unlucky three times out of four. Choosing beats hoping.

What you should actually do if you're starting right now

  1. Take a photo of the wall — daylight, no lamp in the shot.
  2. Read out the hex code (developer eyedropper, ColorZilla or straight from the manufacturer).
  3. On colorhexa.com check the color name and the matching harmony colors.
  4. Decide: do you want harmonious (analogous) or contrast-rich (complementary)?
  5. Open an art platform with a real color filter — or go straight to i-laugh-you and use the color picker over the canvas.
  6. Before buying: print your candidates at full size, hold them to the wall, leave them up for two days. Only then order.
A good wall piece doesn't just look good in daylight. It also has to work at 10 p.m. under the ceiling light. Test that before you pay.

That's the whole method. No interior designer, no subscription. Just a hex code, three terms of color theory and the patience to trial-hang a piece on the wall for two days before buying — a simple paper printout will do in a pinch.

And if you want to try the color picker straight away: head to the i-laugh-you homepage. Enter a hex code — and the system instantly shows you the fragments of the painting that carry that exact color. No catalogue to click through. Color in, art out.
